name: Emeka Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a first-year apprentice with a contractor that rebuilds distribution lines for the power company, around Harlow Cross, which used to be a mill town. Most days we're swapping old poles for new ones, so I'm digging, running the auger, framing crossarms on the ground and sending them up. Kwame, the journeyman who trains me, makes me talk through every step before I do it. It's slow, but I've learned more this year than in two years of college.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ada, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, in a rented terrace by the old canal. We share one car, so some mornings she walks so I can get to the yard. Contractor pay is lower than the power company's own crews, and I've got under a month's money saved. We're fine as long as nothing breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. The hype was mostly about office work anyway, and nobody's building a robot that digs in clay on a wet Tuesday. I'd tell the lads at the yard to stop worrying and keep their heads down for the exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI flopping doesn't make me safe. It just means my problems are the old ones: contractor pay, one car, rent that eats half of everything. Those were there before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the apprenticeship and sit my next module exam in spring. I'd use one of those chat tools now and then to quiz myself on the safety rules, like I do already. And I'd try to get a second-hand bike so Ada isn't walking in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit restless, because okay isn't the same as getting ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine as long as nothing breaks. What broke last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car's gearbox in the summer. Six hundred to fix, and we had to put it on a card. We're still paying that off at about forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being on a contractor rather than the power company itself worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. When the power company's budget is cut, contractors go first. Our contract runs to the end of next year, and nobody at the yard knows if it gets renewed.

say: I'd say the hype was about **office work**, and nobody's robot digs wet clay.
I'd tell the lads to stop worrying and focus on the **exams**.
think: I think my real problems are **contractor pay**, one car and high rent.
I think AI flopping doesn't make me safe; it just leaves the **old problems**.
do: I'd sit my next **module exam** in spring and quiz myself with a chat tool.
I'd buy a **second-hand bike** so my partner isn't walking in the rain.
feel: I'd feel **mostly okay**, but restless because I'm not **getting ahead**.
S0.quote: Contractor pay, one car, rent that eats half of everything. Those were there before anyone said AI.
fieldNote: His pressures are **pre-existing**: a card debt, a shared car, a contract ending next year.
He uses AI tools only for **exam revision**, which fits his steady attitude.
He reads **contractor status** as his biggest risk, ahead of technology.

steps.text: Sit the spring module exam for the line apprenticeship
Use a chat tool to quiz himself on safety rules
Pay off the six hundred gearbox bill at forty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be in the room when the company brings this in. I'd share stuff online about how the planning jobs are going, because people think it's only clever people losing work. It's the schedulers and the storeroom clerks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, I think it's a mixed bag. My hands are still needed on the pole. But if the company plans everything with software, they'll squeeze contractors on time, and that's where corners get cut on safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly, not just pay dues, and go to the meetings. I'd get better with the planning app the crews use, once Kwame shows me how, because whoever reads it fastest gets the good jobs. And I'd try to get the card paid off before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my own spot yet, but I'd be watching the yard closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say the power company uses software to plan the rebuilds. What changes on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The jobs would come in tighter, with times worked out by a computer that's never dug a hole. A pole swap that takes us a day might be booked for five hours. Rushing near live wires is how people get hurt, and you'd be rushing every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if contract crews get squeezed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company bosses who chase the cheapest bid. Not the software, it's just doing what it's told. I'd say that at a meeting too, not just to you.

say: I'd say the **union** must be in the room when the software arrives.
I'd post that **schedulers and clerks** lose work too, not only clever people.
think: I think my **hands** are still needed on the pole for now.
I think software planning will **squeeze contractors** on time and safety.
do: I'd become an **active union member** and attend meetings, not just pay dues.
I'd learn the crew's **planning app** from my trainer and clear the card debt.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy**, not scared for my spot but watching the **yard** closely.
S1.quote: A pole swap that takes us a day might be booked for five hours. Rushing near live wires is how people get hurt, and you'd be rushing every day.
fieldNote: His concern is **safety under time pressure**, not losing his own job.
He blames **cheapest-bid bosses**, not the software, and would say so publicly.
He'll pick up the **planning app** once his trainer shows him, a typical steady move.

steps.text: Attend every union branch meeting instead of just paying dues
Learn the crew planning app with Kwame's help
Clear the credit card balance before saving anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government in on this now, not after. Things like a wage for people pushed out of work, paid for by taxing the companies making the money. I'd be at any march the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years the computers take over planning and design, and then in 2031 the robots come for the climbing. I'd have about three years as a qualified journeyman before that. It's not nothing, but it's not a career either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to finish my apprenticeship early and get my ticket in hand. Then I'd look at substation work or underground cable, because I think those robots would take longer. I'd use the AI tools more, maybe weekly, to learn the theory faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I'm running for a bus I might not catch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still be an apprentice in 2028. What would that mean for finishing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training budgets get cut first when companies panic. If they freeze apprentices in 2028, I'm stuck half-trained with nothing on paper. So I'd be bugging Kwame every week for sign-offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ada talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Ada's job is safer than mine, I think. Kids still need a person in the room, so maybe hers is. We'd probably hold off on the car we wanted and keep every spare bit in the bank.

say: I'd call for a **wage for workers** pushed out, paid by taxing the winners.
I'd join any **union march** about it.
think: I think thinking AI takes **planning and design** first, then robots climb by 2031.
I think three years as a **journeyman** isn't really a career.
do: I'd push to **finish early** and get my ticket in hand.
I'd aim for **substation or underground** work, using AI weekly to learn theory.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, like running for a bus I might not catch.
S2.quote: If they freeze apprentices in 2028, I'm stuck half-trained with nothing on paper.
fieldNote: He sees the risk of being **half-trained** when training budgets freeze.
He looks for the **slowest-to-automate** corners of the trade: substations and underground cable.
Household plan rests on his partner's **teaching assistant job** feeling safer than his.

steps.text: Ask Kwame for weekly sign-offs to finish the apprenticeship early
Study substation theory with an AI tool every week
Join union marches for a wage for displaced workers
Put off buying a second car and bank the spare money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should use it. I'd post about the union pushing for retraining money now. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm qualified with a few years under my belt when the AGI lands. The robots come in 2034, so I'd have about seven years of line work. That's enough to get some savings and a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my ticket on time and then do the substation certificate the year after. I'd start using AI properly in my study, a couple of times a week. I'd also go on the union's training committee if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's a different kind. More like an exam you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2034 look like for you, at 35?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 35 I'd hopefully be in a substation, testing and commissioning. I'd still have thirty years of work left, and nobody has an answer for that. Substations feel like they'll keep people longer, but who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three more years makes all the difference. Is that real or wishful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. It's real because three years is time to finish a certificate. It's wishful because I don't know what the robots will be able to do by then.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** we should use.
I'd post about pushing for **retraining money** now.
think: I think I'd get about **seven years** of line work before robots arrive.
I think that's enough time for some **savings** and a second skill.
do: I'd finish my ticket, then the **substation certificate** the year after.
I'd join the union's **training committee** and study with AI weekly.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, but like before an **exam** you know is coming.
S3.quote: At 35 I'd hopefully be in a substation, testing and commissioning. I'd still have thirty years of work left, and nobody has an answer for that.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **workable plan**: ticket, then a substation certificate.
The worry shifts to the **long tail**: thirty working years left after 2034.
He's honest that the plan is part **wishful thinking**.

steps.text: Take the substation testing certificate the year after qualifying
Join the union's training committee to push retraining money
Study for the certificate with an AI tool twice a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so let's not waste it. I'd want the government and the union to plan it like a big building project. I'd be arguing for that online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a career. I'd be a solid journeyman by 2036, and the robots wouldn't be on poles until 2039. I'd be 40, with time to move into training or supervising them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my ticket, do substations, and then maybe go for a trainer role at the college. Teaching people feels like something that lasts. I'd keep using AI on and off, the way I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but in a fair way. There's a lot of road ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out, would you stay in the trade or move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the trade. I like being outside, and the grid will need rebuilding for all those computers anyway. I'd only move town if the work went somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any plans with Ada?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still plan for a kid in a few years, but I'd want the car paid off and some money saved first. Ada would say I'm being too careful. She's probably right.

say: I'd say there's time to **plan it properly**, like a big building project.
I'd argue online for the **government and union** to plan together.
think: I think ten years feels like a **real career**.
I think at 40 I could move into **training or supervising** robots.
do: I'd get my ticket, do substations, then aim for a **college trainer** role.
I'd keep using AI tools **on and off** as I do now.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy** but in a fair way, with a lot of **road ahead**.
S4.quote: I like being outside, and the grid will need rebuilding for all those computers anyway.
fieldNote: He sees **grid demand** from computers as work for his trade.
His long-term idea is **teaching apprentices**, which he sees as lasting.
He'd still plan a **child**, but only after the car is paid off.

steps.text: Apply for a trainer role at the college after substation work
Pay off the car loan before trying for a child
Keep working full time on the Harlow Cross line crews

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd still be an apprentice, and companies cut training first. What would help is a guarantee that apprentices already signed up get to finish, and some kind of income support while you retrain. That and a second car, if I'm honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old guys. Kwame's got fifteen years in and he's the reason I'm safe on the job. If they push out my trainer Kwame and men like him first, nobody trains people like me.

headlineQuote: If they push out my trainer Kwame and men like him first, nobody trains people like me.
portrait: Emeka is a **first-year apprentice** on a contractor crew rebuilding poles around a former mill town.
He shares **one car** with his partner Ada and has under a month saved.
He's **union-minded** and blames cheapest-bid bosses rather than software.
He uses AI tools **now and then** to revise, and leans more on them as timelines shorten.
He's uneasy in mild pictures and **anxious** under fast AGI, fearing a frozen apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be **half-trained** and companies cut apprentices first.
whatWouldHelp: A **guarantee** that apprentices already signed up get to finish.
